Hammond of Wilmington, whose father was one of the best shots in the East.

"I'll go now." He went off and all that day he sought in vain for a trace of Gerry. He went to all his haunts in the city—he had telephoned to those outside. At night he returned to Alix but it was Mrs. Lansing that received him in the library.

The Judge was tired and his buoyancy had deserted him. He told her of his failure. Mrs. Lansing was thoughtful but not greatly troubled. "Gerry," she said, "has a level head. He can take care of himself." She went to tell Alix that there was no news. When she came back the judge turned to her. "WELL," he asked, "what did she say?"

"Nothing, except that she wanted to know if you had tried the bank."

The judge struck his fist into his left hand. "Never thought of it," he said. "THAT child has a head." He went to the telephone. From the president of the bank he traced the manager, from the manager, the cashier. Yes, Gerry had been at the bank on Saturday. The cashier remembered it because Mr. Lansing had drawn a certain account in full. He would not say how much.

"There," said the judge with a sigh of relief, "that's something. It takes a steady nerve to draw a bank account in full. You must take the news upstairs. I'm off. I'll follow up the clue tomorrow."

There was a new look of content mingled with the worry in Mrs. Lansing's face that made the judge say as he held out his hand in farewell, "Things better?"

Mrs. Lansing understood him. "Yes," she answered, and added, "I've been crying together."

Mrs. Lansing and Alix had never given themselves to each other. There had been no warfare between them but equally there had never been understanding. To Mrs. Lansing's inherent calm, Alix's scintillation had been repellent and Alix before Gerry's mother had felt much the same restraint as before Gerry's old butler. There had been strength in Mrs. Lansing's calm. She had been waiting and now the waiting was over. Alix had given herself fearfully and almost wordlessly into arms that were more than ready and had then poured out her heart in a broken tale that would have confounded any court of Justice but which between women was clearer than logic.

At the end Mrs. Lansing said nothing. Instead she petted Alix, carried her off to bed and kept her there for three days. In her waking hours Alix added spasmodic bits to her confession—sage reflections after the event, dreamy wonders that speculated in the past and the measure of her emotions.

Mrs. Lansing sat and listened and sewed. Her soft brown hair just touched with gray, her calm face with its half-hidden strength, her steady eyes, turned now on Alix, now on her work, brought peace into the room and held it there in spite of the disquieting lack of news of Gerry.

When she spoke at last it was to say half-shyly, "You are stronger than I had thought. I believe every woman at the actual moment of surrender feels an impulse of shame and fear. During that moment desire lets go of her. It's the last chance that fate holds out. The women who fail to take the chance—it seems to me they fail through weakness of spirit and not of flesh. More women are ruined by circumstance than by desire. Women decide to burn their bridges behind them and all the circumstances were against you. There wasn't a loophole in the net. Fate gave you your moment and you tore your way out."

On the fourth day Alix got up but on the fifth she stayed in bed. Mrs. Lansing found her pale and frightened. She had been crying.

"Alix," she whispered, kneeling beside the bed, "what is it?"

Alix told her amid sobs. "Oh, my DEAR," said Mrs. Lansing, throwing her arms around her, "don't cry. Don't worry. The strength will come with the need. In the end you'll be glad. So will Gerry. So will all of us."

"Oh, it isn't that. I'm just thinking and thinking how terrible it would have been if I had run away—really run away. I keep imagining how awful it would have been. It is a nightmare."

"Call it nightmare if you like, sweetheart, but just remember that you are awake."

"Yes," said Alix softly, "I am awake now. I want to watch the Hill mer. It will amuse me. It's long since I have watched for the first buds and the first swallows. I won't mind the melting snow and the mud. It's so long since I've seen clean country mud. I want to smell it."

"You don't know how bleak the Hill can be before the spring comes," objected Mrs. Lansing.

"Will it be any bleaker with me there than when you were alone?" asked Alix.

Mrs. Lansing came over to her and kissed her. "No, DEAR," she said.

Permission FOR the complete reorganization of the Fourth Virginia Infantry was received yesterday by Adjutant General W. W. Sale from the War Department. Failure OF several companies to subscribe TO the dual oath required by the National Defense Act threatened the future existence of the regiment, but an extension of the time limit, which expires to-day, will give the state military authorities an opportunity to bring the organization up to the required strength.

Plans for the rehabilitation of the regiment were discussed at length to-day at meeting of the State Military Board. Owing to a delay in the War Department authorizing an extension of time, the situation, as it concerned the regiment, was acute, and the board was considerably relieved when General Sale received the communication granting the request that he had personally made TO the department last week when he visited Washington.

The board has decided to give the tardy companies another chance to meet the requirements of the National Defense Act, which means that the members OF the company must take an oath to serve the State and national government, and increases the enlistment by extending the time in the reserve TO the three years in active service. The provision of the act is designed to completely Federalize the militia, and all organizations now on the border have subscribed to the oath.

OTHER COMPANIES MAY BE FORMED TO FILL GAPS

Unless the companies take the oath, they will be mustered out and others formed to fill the gaps in the regiment. Regimental officers assert that they can easily get additional companies organized but require time in which to do so. The fact that the Fourth Regiment was not included in the call of the President and the omission of the annual encampment have acted to the detriment of the organization. It has been in the process of rehabilitation for several months, but the recruiting has been slow. The muster-out of one or two companies necessitates an effort being made to fill gaps by the organization of companies in Richmond. The personnel of the regimental officers will not be affected at present.

The State Military Board is planning a new system for the allotment of funds in various companies. On this account the allotment of funds made yesterday was for a period of six months only, being on an old basis of $40 for each dual enlisted member for the year. On the expiration of six months it is expected that the new system will be worked out. Only those companies that have already taken the Federal oath will participate in the distribution of Federal funds.

The board adopted plan for the bonding of officers responsible for all property issued by the State and government. Each responsible officer will be bonded in the sum of $1,000 for the care and preservation of military property placed in his charge. It is believed that this will aid in the proper accounting each year and will have a tendency to make the officers more careful in seeing that the property is kept in the armory and is properly safeguarded. It will also mean that companies with inefficient officers will not be penalized.

Other routine matters were taken up by the board. Those present at the meeting were Governor Stuart, Colonel J. J. James, General C. C. Vaughan, General Sale and Colonel Lane Stern.

He gave warning that plans for the readjustment of the army must be formulated and carried out without delay, and solemnly declared he could not predict that the outlook for the United States would be as bright to-morrow as today. Speaking at the banquet of the Railway Business Men's Association and the Motion Picture Board of Trade, he sounded the keynote of addresses that he will deliver during the next ten days in the midwest.


President in Fighting Mood.


Mr. Wilson was in a fighting mood throughout his address. In speech delivered early in the day he declared he always accepted an invitation to fight. Tonight he told the railway men he was an advocate of peace and had struggled to keep the United States at peace, but he considered the liberty and honor of the nation even more important than peace.


"Woes to any man who plays mad plots, or who seeks to make party, political or personal ambition take precedence over candor, honor and unselfish, bipartisan service," said the president in speaking of his defense plan before the railroad men. He declared that the country expects action. This is a year of accounting and the accounting must be definite on the part of the parties and on the part of every individual who wishes to enjoy the public confidence.


"For my part I hope every man in public life will get what's coming to him," said Mr. Wilson, amid laughter and applause.


Greeted With Enthusiasm.


The president at both banquets and during his day's visit to New York was greeted with enthusiasm. On his ride between the hotels where the banquets were held tonight he was escorted by a band and the Ninth Company Coast Artillery of the New York National Guard. Thousands of persons packed the streets and cheered him as he went by. He cited his recent support of tariff commission as another instance of a change on his part but declared that previously there was no need for such a commission.


Men Clouding the Issue.


Mr. Wilson spoke of men of low character who were clouding the preparedness issue. He declared they were provincial, and that the United States could no longer cut itself off from the rest of the world.


The president vigorously discussed his Mexican policy. He asserted that to invade Mexico would mean the losing of confidence of the rest of the western hemisphere. He cited the freeing of Cuba as an instance of good done by the United States.


"If we are drawn into the male storm which now surges in Europe," the president declared, "we shall not be permitted to do the things we would prefer."
